stem: Which group in an experiment does NOT receive the treatment being tested?
explanation: The control group gets no treatment, so it shows what happens normally. The experimental group is the one that gets the treatment.

stem: A hypothesis must be something that can be tested.
explanation: True. A hypothesis is a testable prediction. If there is no way to test it with an experiment or observations, it is not a scientific hypothesis.

stem: The variable that a scientist purposely changes in an experiment is the
explanation: The independent variable is the one the scientist changes on purpose. The dependent variable is what gets measured.

stem: The variable that a scientist measures to see the effect of the change is the
explanation: The dependent variable is what you measure. It depends on the change you made to the independent variable.

stem: Which statement is a testable hypothesis?
option_b: Science is the most interesting subject.
option_d: If plants receive more hours of light, then they will grow taller.
explanation: An if-then statement that names what is changed (hours of light) and what is measured (plant height) can be tested. The others are opinions.

stem: A good experiment changes several variables at the same time so the results come faster.
explanation: False. A controlled experiment changes only one variable. If several things change at once, you can't tell which one caused the result.

stem: Why do scientists repeat an experiment several times (multiple trials)?
option_a: To make the results more reliable and less affected by chance or mistakes
option_b: To change the independent variable each time
option_c: To prove the hypothesis is always correct
option_d: So they don't need a control group
explanation: Repeating trials shows whether the results are consistent. One trial could be off because of a mistake or chance.

stem: Maria tests whether the amount of salt added to water changes how long the water takes to freeze. What is the independent variable?
option_a: The time it takes to freeze
explanation: Maria changes the amount of salt on purpose, so it is the independent variable. The freezing time is what she measures (dependent variable).

stem: Jake tests whether the brand of paper towel affects how much water it can absorb. What is the dependent variable?
option_b: The size of each paper towel
explanation: Jake measures how much water each towel absorbs, so that is the dependent variable. The brand is what he changes (independent variable).

stem: A student tests how the amount of fertilizer affects the height of bean plants. Which of these should be kept the same (constant) for every plant?
explanation: Everything except the fertilizer should stay the same, like the soil, water, and light. Fertilizer is the independent variable and height is the dependent variable.

stem: A student tests whether water temperature affects how fast an antacid tablet dissolves. Which should be kept constant? Choose all that apply.
option_d: The time it takes to dissolve
explanation: Constants are everything kept the same: the volume of water, the tablet size, and the cup. Water temperature is the independent variable and dissolving time is the dependent variable.

stem: Researchers test whether a new sports drink improves runners' times. Which group is the control group?
option_a: Runners who drink plain water instead of the sports drink
option_b: Runners who drink the sports drink
option_d: Runners who drink two sports drinks
explanation: The control group gets no sports drink (plain water), so the researchers can compare it to the runners who did get the drink.

stem: "If the temperature of water increases, then more sugar will dissolve in it." What is the independent variable in this hypothesis?
option_a: The amount of sugar that dissolves
explanation: In an if-then hypothesis, the "if" part names the independent variable (water temperature) and the "then" part names the dependent variable (sugar dissolved).

stem: The dependent variable is called "dependent" because it depends on the changes made to the independent variable.
explanation: True. The scientist changes the independent variable and watches how the dependent variable responds.

stem: Which is the best way to write a hypothesis so that it can be tested?
option_b: Make it as long as possible
option_c: Write an if-then statement that names the independent and dependent variables
option_d: Ask a question that can't be measured
explanation: An if-then statement that names both variables tells you exactly what to change and what to measure.

stem: What is the experimental group?
option_a: The group that does not get the treatment
option_b: The group the scientist likes best
option_c: The group that is measured first
option_d: The group that receives the change being tested (the independent variable)
explanation: The experimental group gets the treatment or change being tested. The control group does not.

stem: A student's results do not support her hypothesis. What should she do?
option_a: Report the results honestly and revise the hypothesis or test again
option_b: Say the hypothesis was supported anyway
option_c: Change the data so they match the hypothesis
option_d: Throw out the experiment and never report it
explanation: A hypothesis that isn't supported is still useful information. Scientists report their real results and revise their ideas or test again.

stem: A student tests whether music helps plants grow. Plant A gets music, sits in a sunny window, and gets 50 mL of water a day. Plant B gets no music, sits in a dark closet, and gets 50 mL of water a day. What is the biggest problem with this experiment?
option_a: Both plants got the same amount of water
option_b: Two variables changed (music and light), so the student can't tell which caused any difference
option_c: The student should have used a different kind of plant for each group
explanation: Both music and light are different between the plants. If Plant A grows more, it could be from the light, not the music. Only one variable should change.

stem: Which fertilizer experiment would give the most reliable results?
option_a: 1 plant with fertilizer and 1 plant without
option_c: 30 plants with fertilizer and 30 without, repeated several times
option_d: 30 plants with fertilizer and 1 plant without
explanation: Large, equal groups and repeated trials make it much less likely that one unusual plant decides the result.

stem: After asking five friends, a student claims that eating breakfast causes higher test scores. What is the best criticism of this claim?
option_b: The student should have asked only one friend
option_c: Five friends is a small sample, and nothing was controlled, so the survey can't show what causes higher scores
option_d: The claim is correct because friends always tell the truth
explanation: A tiny sample with no control group and no constants can't show cause and effect. Other things, like sleep or studying, could explain the scores.

stem: A student wants to test whether the amount of light affects how fast duckweed grows. Which are needed for a controlled experiment? Choose all that apply.
option_a: A control group of duckweed under normal light
option_b: Several groups under different amounts of light
option_c: The same water temperature for every group
option_d: A different kind of plant in each group
option_e: Measuring growth the same way every day
explanation: A controlled experiment needs a control group, experimental groups that differ only in light, constants like water temperature, and the same way of measuring. Using different plants would add a second variable.

stem: In an experiment, the independent variable is the amount of exercise and the dependent variable is resting heart rate. Which hypothesis matches this experiment?
option_b: If resting heart rate increases, then people will exercise more.
option_c: If people eat more, then their heart rate will increase.
option_d: If people exercise more, then their resting heart rate will decrease.
explanation: The "if" part should name the independent variable (exercise) and the "then" part the dependent variable (resting heart rate).

stem: A student grows plants with different amounts of fertilizer: 0 g → 5 cm, 5 g → 9 cm, 10 g → 12 cm, 20 g → 4 cm. Which conclusion is best supported?
option_a: Growth increased up to 10 g of fertilizer, but 20 g reduced growth
option_b: More fertilizer always makes plants grow taller
option_c: Fertilizer had no effect on growth
option_d: Plants grow best with no fertilizer
explanation: Height went up from 0 g to 10 g but dropped at 20 g, so too much fertilizer hurt growth. The data don't show that more is always better.

stem: Why is it important to change only one variable in an experiment?
option_a: So the experiment takes less time
option_b: So any difference in the results can be linked to that one variable
option_c: So you don't need to measure anything
option_d: So the hypothesis is always supported
explanation: If only one thing changes, that change is the only explanation for different results. That is what makes it a controlled experiment.

stem: Which of these is a biotic (living) factor?
explanation: A mushroom is a living fungus. Sunlight, water, and rocks are abiotic (nonliving) factors.

stem: All living things are made of one or more cells.
explanation: True. Every living thing, from bacteria to trees to people, is made of at least one cell.

stem: Which of these is an abiotic (nonliving) factor?
explanation: Temperature is a physical condition, not a living thing. Grass, bacteria, and deer are all biotic.

stem: Keeping a stable internal environment, like a steady body temperature, is called
explanation: Homeostasis is how living things keep conditions inside their bodies stable even when the outside changes.

stem: Sweating on a hot day is an example of which characteristic of life?
explanation: Sweating cools the body so its temperature stays steady. That is homeostasis.

stem: Fire is alive because it grows, uses oxygen, and can spread.
explanation: False. Fire shows some features of life, but it is not made of cells, has no DNA, and cannot reproduce on its own.

stem: All the chemical reactions a living thing uses to build up or break down materials and obtain energy are called its
explanation: Metabolism is the set of chemical reactions that let an organism get and use energy.

stem: A sunflower turns to face the sun as it moves across the sky. Which characteristic of life does this show?
explanation: Sunlight is a stimulus, and the sunflower turning toward it is a response.

stem: A tadpole changes into a frog. Which characteristic of life does this show?
explanation: Living things grow and develop, and the change from tadpole to frog is development.

stem: One bacterium splits into two new bacteria. Which characteristic of life does this show?
explanation: Making new organisms is reproduction. Bacteria reproduce asexually by splitting in two.

stem: Which characteristic of life explains why offspring look like their parents?
option_c: Living things have a genetic code (DNA) that is passed to offspring
explanation: DNA carries the instructions for traits, and it is passed from parents to offspring.

stem: Which of these are characteristics of ALL living things? Choose all that apply.
option_b: Can move from place to place
explanation: All living things are made of cells, use energy, reproduce, and respond to their environment. Many living things, like plants, don't move from place to place or have a heart.

stem: Over many generations, a population of bacteria becomes resistant to an antibiotic. Which characteristic of life does this show?
option_d: Changing over time (evolving) as a group
explanation: A population that changes over many generations is evolving. Individual bacteria don't change, but the group does.

stem: A seed sitting in a packet is nonliving because it is not growing.
explanation: False. A seed is alive but dormant. It is made of cells, has DNA, and will grow when it gets water and warmth.

stem: A salt crystal grows larger in salty water. Why is it still NOT alive?
option_a: It is not made of cells and has no DNA
explanation: Growing alone doesn't make something alive. A crystal is not made of cells, has no DNA, and can't reproduce.

stem: Which pair from a pond has one biotic factor and one abiotic factor?
option_b: A duck and the amount of oxygen dissolved in the water
explanation: The duck is biotic (living) and dissolved oxygen is abiotic (nonliving). The other pairs are both living or both nonliving.

stem: A fallen leaf lying on the forest floor is best described as
option_a: abiotic, because it was never alive
option_c: biotic, because it came from a living thing
explanation: Biotic factors include living things and things that came from living things, like fallen leaves, dead logs, and animal waste.

stem: Viruses have genetic material, but they are not made of cells and can only reproduce inside a host cell. Most biologists classify viruses as
option_a: living, because they have genetic material
option_b: not living, because they are too small to see
option_d: not living, because they are not made of cells and cannot reproduce on their own
explanation: Having genetic material isn't enough. Viruses are not cells and can't reproduce or use energy on their own, so most biologists don't consider them alive.

stem: A student finds an unknown object in a pond. Which observation would be the strongest evidence that it is alive?
option_a: Under a microscope, it is made of cells
option_d: It gets bigger after soaking in water
explanation: Being made of cells is a characteristic of all living things. Nonliving things can move, be warm, or swell in water.

stem: A student says, "A car is alive because it uses energy from gasoline and it moves." Which is the best response?
option_a: The student is right; using energy proves something is alive
option_b: Using energy is only one characteristic; a car is not made of cells, has no DNA, and cannot reproduce
option_c: A car is alive only when it is running
option_d: Cars are alive because people built them
explanation: Something must show all the characteristics of life to be living. A car shows one or two, but not the rest.

stem: A student puts yeast in sugar water. Bubbles of gas form, the number of yeast cells increases, and the yeast is seen as tiny cells under a microscope. Which characteristics of life do these observations show? Choose all that apply.
explanation: The bubbles come from yeast breaking down sugar for energy, more cells means reproduction, and the microscope shows cells. Nothing here shows evolution or homeostasis.

stem: Your body temperature stays near 37 °C whether it is 10 °C or 30 °C outside. Which explanation is best?
option_a: Your body grows faster when it is warm
option_b: Your body evolves to match the weather each day
option_c: Your body responds by sweating or shivering to keep its internal temperature stable (homeostasis)
option_d: Your cells stop working when it is cold
explanation: Sweating and shivering are responses that keep your internal temperature steady. Keeping internal conditions stable is homeostasis.

stem: Why do biologists use several characteristics, not just one, to decide whether something is alive?
option_a: Because one characteristic is too easy to measure
option_b: Because only animals have characteristics of life
option_c: Because living things never show more than one characteristic
option_d: Because some nonliving things show one characteristic, like fire growing or crystals getting bigger
explanation: Fire, crystals, and machines can each show one feature of life. Something is alive only if it shows all of them.

stem: A mule cannot have offspring, yet it is alive. What is the best explanation?
option_a: A mule is made of cells, uses energy, grows, and responds; reproduction is a characteristic of a species, not of every single individual
option_b: Reproduction is not a characteristic of life
option_c: A mule is not really alive
option_d: Mules reproduce by splitting in two
explanation: A mule shows the other characteristics of life. Reproduction describes living things as a group; some individuals can't reproduce and are still alive.

stem: Which part of the microscope do you look through?
explanation: The ocular lens, or eyepiece, is at the top. You look through it, and it magnifies the image (usually 10×).

stem: Which part is the flat platform that holds the slide?
explanation: The stage holds the slide under the objective lens. Stage clips keep the slide in place.

stem: You should carry a microscope with one hand on the arm and the other hand under the base.
explanation: True. Two hands, one on the arm and one under the base, keep the microscope from being dropped.

stem: Which knob should be used only on low power and never on high power?
explanation: The coarse adjustment knob moves the stage a lot and is used only on low power. On high power, use only the fine adjustment knob.

stem: What does the diaphragm do?
option_a: Controls the amount of light that passes through the specimen
explanation: The diaphragm opens and closes to control how much light reaches the specimen.

stem: What is the job of the stage clips?
option_b: To hold the slide in place on the stage
explanation: Stage clips hold the slide still on the stage so it doesn't slide around while you focus.

stem: When using the high-power objective, you should focus with the coarse adjustment knob.
explanation: False. On high power, use only the fine adjustment knob. The coarse knob moves too far and can crash the objective into the slide.

stem: A microscope has a 10× ocular lens and a 40× objective lens. What is the total magnification?
explanation: Total magnification = ocular × objective: 10 × 40 = 400×.

stem: A microscope has a 15× ocular lens and a 10× objective lens. What is the total magnification?
explanation: Multiply the two lenses: 15 × 10 = 150×.

stem: What does the revolving nosepiece do?
option_c: Holds the objective lenses and turns to switch between them
explanation: The nosepiece holds the objective lenses and rotates so you can change magnification.

stem: When you first focus on a new slide, which objective should be in place?
explanation: Start on the lowest power. It has the widest field of view, which makes the specimen easiest to find.

stem: A slide with the letter "e" on it is placed on the stage right side up. How does the "e" look through the microscope?
explanation: The lenses flip the image, so it looks upside down and backward (inverted).

stem: While looking through the microscope, you move the slide to the left. Which way does the image move?
explanation: Because the image is inverted, it moves the opposite way you move the slide.

stem: When you switch from low power to high power, the field of view gets smaller and you see less of the specimen.
explanation: True. High power makes things look bigger, but you see a smaller area of the slide.

stem: Which parts of a microscope contain lenses that magnify the specimen? Choose all that apply.
explanation: The ocular lens and the objective lenses magnify. The stage holds the slide, the diaphragm controls light, and the base supports the microscope.

stem: What does the light source (lamp) do?
option_c: Shines light up through the specimen so you can see it
explanation: Light from the lamp passes up through the specimen and the lenses to your eye.

stem: Why must a specimen on a slide be very thin?
option_a: So it won't stick to the slide
option_b: So it fits under the stage clips
option_d: So light can pass through it
explanation: A light microscope works by shining light through the specimen. A thick specimen blocks the light and looks dark.

stem: After switching to high power, a student's image is in focus but looks too dark. What should the student do?
option_a: Open the diaphragm to let in more light
option_c: Take the slide off the stage
option_d: Switch to a different ocular lens
explanation: High power lets in less light. Opening the diaphragm sends more light through the specimen.

stem: A cell is easy to see on low power but disappears when the student switches to high power. What is the most likely reason?
option_b: The cell was not centered before switching, and the high-power field of view is smaller
option_d: The diaphragm was closed all the way
explanation: High power shows a smaller area. If the cell wasn't in the center first, it can end up outside the field of view.

stem: Which order of steps is correct for viewing a slide?
option_a: Place the slide, switch to high power, focus with the coarse knob
option_b: Start on high power, focus with the coarse knob, then place the slide
option_c: Place the slide, start on low power, focus with the coarse knob, center the specimen, switch to high power, focus with the fine knob
option_d: Focus with the fine knob, place the slide, then turn on the light
explanation: Start low, focus with coarse, center, then switch to high and use only the fine knob.

stem: A student cracked a slide while focusing on high power. What mistake did the student most likely make?
option_d: Used the coarse adjustment knob on high power
explanation: The coarse knob moves the stage a long way. On high power the objective is very close to the slide, so it can crash into it.

stem: Which of these are proper ways to use and care for a microscope? Choose all that apply.
option_b: Use the coarse knob on high power
option_c: Clean the lenses with lens paper
option_d: Put it away with the highest-power objective in place
explanation: Start on low power, clean lenses only with lens paper, and carry with two hands. Never use the coarse knob on high power, and put the microscope away on low power.

stem: Compared with low power, what do you see on high power?
option_a: A larger image, a smaller field of view, and a dimmer view
option_b: A smaller image, a larger field of view, and a brighter view
option_c: The same image size with more light
option_d: A larger image and a larger field of view
explanation: High power makes the specimen look bigger, but you see a smaller area and less light gets through.

stem: A microscope's total magnification is 400×, and the ocular lens is 10×. Which objective lens is in place?
explanation: Total = ocular × objective, so 400 = 10 × objective. The objective is 40×.

stem: Data that are recorded as numbers, like length or mass, are called
explanation: Quantitative data are numbers (quantities). Qualitative data describe qualities like color or texture.

stem: On a line graph, the independent variable is usually placed on the x-axis.
explanation: True. The independent variable goes on the x-axis (horizontal) and the dependent variable on the y-axis (vertical).

stem: What should every graph include?
option_c: A title and labeled axes with units
option_d: The hypothesis written in the middle
explanation: A title tells what the graph is about, and labeled axes with units tell what was measured and how.

stem: Which type of graph is best for showing how something changes over time?
explanation: A line graph connects data points so the change over time is easy to see.

stem: Which type of graph is best for comparing separate groups, like the number of birds of each species at a feeder?
explanation: A bar graph compares separate categories side by side.

stem: "The leaf is 6 cm long" is a qualitative observation.
explanation: False. It is quantitative because it uses a number with a unit. A qualitative observation would be "the leaf is dark green."

stem: Which type of graph is best for showing parts of a whole, like the percent of a diet made of protein, fat, and carbohydrates?
option_c: Bar graph with time on the x-axis
explanation: A pie chart shows how a whole is divided into parts, usually as percents.

stem: A plant's height was 2 cm on day 0, 5 cm on day 5, 9 cm on day 10, and 14 cm on day 15. Which describes the trend?
explanation: Each measurement is larger than the one before, so the plant grew taller over time.

stem: Three trials took 12 seconds, 14 seconds, and 16 seconds. What is the mean (average) time?
explanation: Add the trials and divide by how many there are: (12 + 14 + 16) ÷ 3 = 42 ÷ 3 = 14 seconds.

stem: A student graphs the amount of fertilizer (g) and plant height (cm). What belongs on the y-axis?
explanation: Plant height is the dependent variable (what was measured), so it goes on the y-axis.

stem: Which is the best title for a graph of how temperature affects the number of times crickets chirp per minute?
option_a: The Effect of Temperature on Cricket Chirps per Minute
explanation: A good title names both variables, usually as "The Effect of [independent variable] on [dependent variable]."

stem: In a data table, which variable usually goes in the first (left) column?
explanation: The independent variable goes in the first column, and the measurements of the dependent variable go in the columns next to it.

stem: Which of these are quantitative observations? Choose all that apply.
explanation: Quantitative observations use numbers and units: 25 g, 8 cm, and 22 °C. Color and texture are qualitative.

stem: A conclusion should state whether the data support or do not support the hypothesis.
explanation: True. A conclusion answers the question the experiment asked, using the data as evidence.

stem: Why should units be included on the axes of a graph?
option_a: To make the graph look longer
option_b: Units are only needed in the title
option_c: So readers know exactly what was measured and how (for example, cm or m)
option_d: So the graph can skip the title
explanation: Without units, a reader can't tell whether 5 means 5 cm, 5 m, or 5 seconds.

stem: Enzyme reactions per minute were 4 at 10 °C, 8 at 20 °C, 12 at 30 °C, and 16 at 40 °C. About how many reactions per minute would you predict at 25 °C?
explanation: 25 °C is halfway between 20 °C (8) and 30 °C (12), so about 10 reactions per minute.

stem: On a line graph, the line slopes downward from left to right. What does this show?
option_a: As the independent variable increases, the dependent variable increases
option_d: As the independent variable increases, the dependent variable decreases
explanation: A downward slope means that as the x-axis value goes up, the y-axis value goes down.

stem: Students who studied 1, 2, 3, and 4 hours scored 60, 70, 80, and 85 on a test. Which conclusion is best supported?
option_a: Test scores increased as study time increased
option_c: Study time has no effect on test scores
option_d: Test scores decreased as study time increased
explanation: Scores went up with each extra hour of study. The data don't prove what would happen beyond 4 hours.

stem: Five trials gave these results: 15, 16, 15, 42, and 16. What is the best way to handle the 42?
option_a: Use only the 42 because it is the largest
option_b: Treat it as a likely error (an outlier), check what went wrong, and repeat that trial
option_c: Average all five and ignore any problems
option_d: Throw out all the data and start over
explanation: 42 is far from the other results, so something may have gone wrong. Scientists check for errors and repeat the trial instead of hiding or blindly using it.

stem: A bar graph's y-axis starts at 90 instead of 0, so scores of 92 and 95 look very different. What is the problem with this graph?
option_a: The bars are the wrong color
option_c: The scale exaggerates a small difference and can mislead readers
explanation: Starting the axis at 90 makes a 3-point difference look huge. A fair scale shows differences at their true size.

stem: Which is the clearest and most complete way to communicate the results of an experiment?
option_a: A drawing of the lab equipment
option_b: A paragraph of opinions about the experiment
option_c: Only the raw numbers written in a list
option_d: A labeled data table and graph with a short conclusion that tells whether the hypothesis was supported
explanation: Organized data, a labeled graph, and a concise conclusion let others see the evidence and what it means.

stem: Which of these should appear on every line graph? Choose all that apply.
option_d: An evenly spaced scale on each axis
option_e: A list of the lab materials
explanation: A complete graph has a title, both axes labeled with units, and evenly spaced scales. The materials list belongs in the procedure.

stem: Plants with fertilizer grew 10, 12, and 11 cm. Plants without fertilizer grew 10, 11, and 10 cm. Which conclusion is best?
option_a: Plants with fertilizer grew slightly taller on average (11 cm vs. about 10.3 cm), but the difference is small, so more trials are needed
option_d: The results prove fertilizer always works
explanation: The averages are close, and there were only three plants per group. The data hint at a small effect, but more trials would make the conclusion stronger.

stem: A student measures the temperature of a cup of hot water every minute for 10 minutes. Which graph best shows the results?
option_a: A line graph with temperature on the x-axis and time on the y-axis
option_b: A line graph with time on the x-axis and temperature on the y-axis
option_d: A bar graph of the cup's color
explanation: Temperature changing over time is continuous data, so a line graph fits. Time is the independent variable, so it goes on the x-axis.
